title.en: The Nuclear Question: Taiwan's Energy Trilemma
The Day the Reactor Went Quiet

A2.text: On May 17, 2025, Taiwan turned off its last nuclear reactor. Just three months later, voters were asked to turn it back on completely. So what really changed?

B1.text: Picture the headline from three months ago. On 17 May 2025, Taiwan eventually switched off its last working reactor, though that was not quite the end of this narrative.

B2.text: Just three months after formally switching off its final reactor, Taiwan asked the electorate whether nuclear power should resume. What shifted in that short interval is precisely what this discussion unpacks.

A2.text: SDG 7 means safe, reliable, modern energy for everyone. Today we look at nuclear power through one simple idea. There are three goals, and they are hard to reach together.

B1.text: SDG 7 promises affordable, reliable and clean energy for all of us. Today we will use nuclear power as a lens for the energy trilemma, three goals that are hard to balance.

B2.text: SDG 7 calls for affordable, reliable and sustainable energy for everyone, although this talk narrows that lens onto nuclear power specifically. It uses the so-called energy trilemma, three aims that seldom align.

A2.text: This story starts about ten years ago. In 2016, Taiwan chose a bold new plan. There would be no nuclear power after 2025. Today we look back at that long countdown.

B1.text: This policy actually goes back about ten years, to 2016, when a new government promised no nuclear power after 2025. A 2017 law then made that promise official.

B2.text: Despite sounding recent, this policy is actually a decade in the making. A party voted into office in 2016 on a nuclear-free pledge saw that commitment codified into statute the following year.

stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

A2.text: On May 17, 2025, Maanshan's last reactor shut down. This ended over 40 years of nuclear power here. Nuclear made only 4 percent of our power in 2024.

B1.text: On 17 May 2025, Reactor Two at Maanshan shut down for good. Nuclear power, which had supplied about 4 percent of 2024 generation, has now left Taiwan's grid for good.

B2.text: By 17 May 2025, the second reactor at Maanshan had been decommissioned permanently, closing the chapter entirely. Nuclear generation, once around 4 percent of 2024's total, vanished from the grid overnight.

title.en: Who Fills the Gap Nuclear Leaves

A2.text: Gas and coal made over 80 percent of our power in 2024. Nuclear then stopped. Gas and coal filled most of that gap, not renewable energy.

B1.text: With renewables still behind their own targets, fossil fuels have absorbed most of what nuclear left behind. In 2024, gas and coal already supplied 83 percent of our electricity.

B2.text: Since renewable capacity is still lagging behind its own build-out schedule, fossil-fuel plants have picked up nearly everything that nuclear power used to provide. More than 80 percent of 2024's electricity therefore came from coal and gas.

title.en: Voters Say Yes, the Threshold Says No

A2.text: People's views also moved. In August 2025, most voters who voted said yes to the plant. But not enough people voted, so the vote failed by law.

B1.text: Public opinion has clearly shifted. In the August referendum, 74.2 percent of votes cast said yes to restarting Maanshan, yet turnout fell short of the legal threshold required to pass.

B2.text: Sentiment toward nuclear power has plainly reversed in recent months. Although 74.2 percent of votes cast favoured reviving Maanshan, overall turnout never actually reached the level Taiwan's law demands.

A2.text: What did Taiwan build instead? Over the past ten years, Taiwan added new gas terminals. It also built more wind turbines and solar panels.

B1.text: Taiwan has changed its power mix over the past ten years. Gas import terminals, offshore wind and solar capacity have all grown, even as nuclear power was phased out completely.

B2.text: Even while retiring nuclear capacity across a full decade, Taiwan has hardly been idle elsewhere. LNG terminals, offshore turbines and solar arrays have been expanded considerably across that same stretch.

A2.text: Nuclear and clean energy both release almost no carbon. Coal and gas release much more. So using more coal and gas raises Taiwan's total carbon output.

B1.text: Nuclear power and renewables both release essentially no carbon, quite unlike coal and gas. So using more coal or gas instead of nuclear power carries a real emissions cost.

B2.text: Both nuclear and renewable generation emit negligible carbon at the point of production, a trait fossil fuels simply lack. Displacing nuclear specifically with coal or gas therefore carries a measurable climate cost.

title.zh: 穩定基載對上看天吃飯

A2.text: Nuclear power runs all day and night, no matter the weather. Solar and wind power change with the sun and wind constantly. That makes the electric grid harder to balance.

B1.text: Nuclear power runs steadily in any weather, a quality engineers call baseload. Solar and wind output rises and falls with the sun and wind, which makes grid balancing harder.

B2.text: Unlike weather-dependent sources, nuclear plants deliver steady output no matter the conditions outside, a trait engineers call baseload power. Solar and wind, by contrast, rise and fall constantly, which complicates balancing supply and demand.

A2.text: One option is to restart the reactor. This could cut carbon and cost fast, but it needs new safety inspections. Nobody agrees on how long that should take.

B1.text: Restarting the plant, as the referendum proposed, could cut emissions and cost quickly. But it would also require new safety reviews and a level of public trust that remains uncertain.

B2.text: Had the referendum succeeded, reactivating the plant could have trimmed both emissions and cost fairly quickly. Doing so would nonetheless demand fresh safety audits and a degree of public confidence not yet secured.

title.en: Option Two: Race Renewables and Storage
title.zh: 選項二：加速再生能源與儲能

A2.text: A second option is building clean energy and storage faster. This choice is popular and very green. But it is already behind its own plan.

B1.text: Building more renewables and storage instead is popular and very clean. But that plan is already behind its own delivery date, so it will not fix things instantly.

B2.text: Pouring resources into renewables and storage instead carries real popularity and genuine public appeal. Nonetheless, that expansion already trails its own rollout plan, so it is no quick fix either.

title.en: Option Three: Lean on Imported Gas
title.zh: 選項三：倚賴進口天然氣

A2.text: A third option is using more imported gas as a bridge fuel. It is cleaner than coal. But Taiwan already imports almost all of its energy.

B1.text: Leaning further on imported gas is cleaner than coal and flexible to run. Yet it would deepen Taiwan's already heavy dependence on energy that must be shipped in from abroad.

B2.text: Turning further toward imported gas burns cleaner than coal and adapts more easily to changing electricity demand. Doing so, however, would deepen an import dependence that already leaves Taiwan strategically exposed.

A2.text: Taiwan has only about two weeks of energy reserves. That means we cannot lose any power source easily. If one ship is delayed, that safety margin gets even smaller.

B1.text: Taiwan can rely on stored energy reserves for only about two weeks, while imports supply nearly 97 percent of everything it uses. A delay in just one shipment tightens that margin a lot.

B2.text: Taiwan's workable reserves stretch across roughly two weeks, while imports account for nearly 97 percent of total energy supply. Should a single shipment be delayed, that safety margin shrinks almost instantly.

A2.text: Taipower has lost huge amounts of money for years. If prices stay too low, the company cannot pay for new power plants and storage.

B1.text: Taipower has already lost about NT$418 billion in total losses. If it keeps paying for new plants while prices stay low, its financial problems will only keep getting worse.

B2.text: Taipower's cumulative losses have swollen to roughly NT$418 billion, a figure that keeps climbing. Continuing to fund new capacity without any change to sensitive prices will only deepen that hole.

title.en: The Carbon Math Still Has to Work
title.zh: 碳排的數學還是要成立

A2.text: The carbon math still has to work. Even without enough new clean power, Taiwan must cut carbon fast. Otherwise gas and coal use will keep rising.

B1.text: Meeting climate goals means cutting the fossil share of the grid substantially. But neither a nuclear restart nor the renewable build-out can happen fast enough to avoid leaning on gas.

B2.text: Climate commitments cannot be met without a substantial cut to the fossil share of generation. Neither a nuclear revival nor a faster rollout of renewables can arrive quickly enough to prevent continued reliance on gas.

A2.text: So no single energy choice wins on all three goals. A safer choice can cost much more money. A cheaper choice can raise carbon. That is the real trilemma.

B1.text: These three pressures pull against each other constantly. If Taiwan improves security by restarting a reactor, it can ease cost worries too, yet public trust and review time both suffer.

B2.text: These three pressures constantly work against one another. Only when security, cost and emissions are jointly satisfied will any single pathway qualify as genuinely sustainable, and no option secures every goal for free.

A2.text: To wrap up, Taiwan ended nuclear power right on time. Then voters almost changed that choice months later. The trilemma shows why neither choice was ever simple.

B1.text: In short, Taiwan retired its nuclear plants right when the law required. Public support for reversing course then surged only months afterward, and the trilemma is exactly why no option was easy.

B2.text: In summary, Taiwan retired nuclear power precisely as scheduled, only for voters to nearly reverse that outcome within months. The trilemma clarifies why no available option was ever going to be straightforward.

title.en: Engineers Will Decide the Next Round
title.zh: 工程師將決定下一回合

A2.text: This matters to you directly, right here in this room. Future engineers will design the reactors, grids and storage. Slogans will not do that work for us.

B1.text: This whole issue is not abstract for the people sitting here today. It will be you, rather than campaign slogans, who eventually decides how the reactors, grids and storage evolve.

B2.text: This dilemma bears directly on those seated in this room. Engineers, rather than campaign slogans, will ultimately be the ones designing whichever reactors, grids or storage systems eventually resolve this tension.

title.en: Read the Data Before You Pick a Side

A2.text: Read the real numbers before you choose a side. Ask what problem each technology actually solves. Do not just pick a team to cheer for.

B1.text: Let's read the emissions, cost and security data closely before choosing a side. Ask what problem a given technology solves, instead of simply picking a team to support.

B2.text: Let's commit to interrogating the emissions, cost and security figures first, before anything else. What genuinely matters is which problem a given technology solves, not which side feels more appealing to support.

title.en: Let the Next Vote Be an Informed One
title.zh: 讓下一次投票更加知情

A2.text: The next vote, or the next reactor design, will eventually be decided by data or by loud slogans. Let's choose data instead. That choice is what should end this talk.

B1.text: Let's leave with one clear thought before we conclude. The next vote, or the next grid blueprint, will be decided with better evidence or with louder slogans, and that choice now belongs to you.

B2.text: Let's close on a single guiding thought. Whichever comes next, a referendum or a grid blueprint, will be shaped by rigorous evidence or by persuasive slogans, and that outcome is now down to you.
